The freedom we carry in these words is not a break with human nature but a return to its purity; it is not a rebellion against the human being but a recovery of his essence. When a person is pushed to abandon his meaning in the name of liberation, that is stripping, not freeing; emptying, not empowering. How easy it is to seduce minds with slogans, and how hard it is to bring souls to take a stand. True freedom does not wrestle with morals; it leans on them. It does not dissolve differences; it puts them in their proper place, preserving balance and protecting meaning.

When nations lose their moral compass, they turn into moving bodies without a soul and multiplying voices without a direction. The clamour of pulpits does not create values, and an abundance of terms does not save a destiny. Nations endure only through what they preserve within: a cohesive family, a modesty that guards behaviour, and a chastity that prevents collapse before it appears. Wherever these pillars are torn down in the name of freedom, disintegration begins from within and the foundations erode until the fall becomes a course, not an accident.

That is why these words do not deliver a speech or seek applause; they take a stand. They do not hand over a banner; they light a torch. They do not beg for agreement; they entrust a responsibility. The freedom we believe in is not inherited as texts but passed on as values, and it does not settle in constitutions until it has settled in souls. In this way meaning stays alive, values stay active, and freedom remains a name worth living by, not a slogan raised and then forgotten.

And yet the word that wishes to last is not made sufficient by eloquence until it takes root in conduct, nor protected by the ring of its phrasing until it becomes an order within and a measure in action. The freedom we affirm here is not vanity on display but dignity in the home; not noise from the pulpits but tranquillity in the conscience.

When a nation protects its family, it protects its state; when it honours modesty, it honours the future; and when it cares for its values, it establishes justice without strain. Then freedom stands upright at its full height, becoming a guardian of dignity, a ladder to civilisation, and a torch that the winds of confusion cannot put out and the dust of desire cannot obscure. This is how the days are written in the record of nations as a book of light.

sumuw-al-atifa.title: The Height of Emotion and the Sovereignty of Love
sumuw-al-atifa.sub: When Love Is Awareness… Not Impulse
sumuw-al-atifa.d1: “The Height of Emotion and the Sovereignty of Love” is a book by Dr. Yousef Ahmad Al-Maiari.
desc: To the word: not when it is merely spoken, but when it summons itself and rises from its silence as something inevitable, not out of the slackness of habit. To the word when it comes from the mouth of time, weighed down by its experiences and carried by its questions, not from the complacent mouth of routine. To the word when it falls on the rock of meaning like a pickaxe, and the meaning splits open as truth splits from falsehood; it does not bounce back as an echo, borrow worn-out images, or make itself at home with falsehood.

To the word when it comes down on the mind like a hammer on an anvil, recasting it rather than decorating it, and tearing illusion away rather than humouring it. This is a book that is not opened but entered by force; it does not prepare the ground, it makes its case; it does not ask permission, it stands firm — firm as a trace that cannot be erased, as a crack in the maps of the heart that cannot be covered over; not to decorate the path but to reveal it, not to console the reader but to burden him with meaning and its consequences.

Here language begins at its greatest tension, from an edge beyond which there is no return, a point after which, once speech is uttered, everything before it is overturned. Here the word is written as a covenant, not a phrase, and the banner of nearness is raised as a responsibility to be carried, not a title to be read. It is not a slogan to be waved, but a touchstone that separates truth from falsehood, a threshold that only those who accept the cost and understand its price can cross.

At the heart of this book the height of emotion appears — not as blind impulse but as high moral awareness; not as passing infatuation but as the sovereignty of love over one’s own soul before anyone else’s. Here love is a refined strength, emotion is a scale, and the heart is a place of trust, not a stage for display. A covenant either turns into a loyalty that holds firm through exhaustion, or falls as a scandal at the test; and the banner is either raised as a true bond of the heart, or lowered as a worn-out claim.

To those who know that love that is never tested falls, and that love not weighted with loyalty slips away; that longing not refined by constancy disperses, and longing not bound by a covenant changes. To those who plant the banner in their hearts before they set it up in lines of writing, and seal the covenant in their conscience before they proclaim it on the road. Here words are not read by the eyes but carried as covenants and debts: a word is either a covenant that is sealed, and the heart is sealed with it, or a promise that breaks apart, and the road breaks apart with it.

This is a book that does not soften and so become cheap, does not flatter and so betray, and does not borrow glitter to hide the truth. It brings the truth stripped of ornament and free of bargaining, heavy as a stone placed on its scale, firm as a mountain set in its place. It does not weigh a word by its ring but by its truth; it does not set up an image for its splendour but for its clarity. There is no glory in an evasive obscurity, no merit in a roundabout justification, and no honour for an idea that glitters on the surface and fades in the depths.

To those who are weary of a language that promises and does not deliver, that claims and does not rise, that circles around itself and goes nowhere: this book comes as a statement that decides without injustice and connects without cutting off, setting the balance between strength and kindness, between firmness and safety. It is an honesty that, when spoken, binds; when weighed, sets things right; and when asked to take a stand, steps forward and does not hold back.

And to those who will come after the crowds have dispersed, the noise has broken and the voices have faded, when nothing remains but the trace as witness and nothing stands but the truth: these are not pages to be turned but positions to be taken; not a memory to be kept but an obligation to be recognised and honoured. Whoever enters this book enters a covenant that is not broken and a pact that is not undone: to carry honesty as a direction, not an ornament; to raise nearness as a trust, not a placard; and to bear longing as constancy, not a whim; as resolve, not a passing glance.

Here the word is an oath that binds once it is sworn, the covenant a pact that holds once it is tied, and the banner a trust for which one is answerable once it is raised. From here the book begins as a condition that is not postponed, a limit that is not crossed and a road that does not end: clarity is a principle not to be neglected, taking a stand is a resolve not to be delayed, and honesty is a light that, when it shines, burns away falsehood and banishes lies; and when it is absent, meaning disappears with it, the scale falls, and the human being comes apart.

From this threshold the word moves from a sound that is said and then forgotten to a trace that is established; from a sound that is heard and then ends to a landmark drawn in awareness in a way that cannot be wronged. It stops being an ornament of speech and becomes an order that truly binds, carrying a person from the place of watching to the station of standing up, and from the circle of receiving to the field of commitment. Speech is not measured by how harmonious it sounds, but by its power to turn the course of days and to shake a stillness that hid behind the name of wisdom when it was, in truth, surrender.

The word here does not flatter and so fawn, nor circle and so equivocate; it confronts and so speaks plainly, names and so corrects, and puts the truth in its proper place in a way that cannot be undone. It rejects a language that sedates and lulls, that decorates and falsifies, that justifies and postpones; and it chooses a language that wakes and moves, moves and changes, changes and decides.

When this understanding settles completely in the heart, the covenant becomes a system of values that tolerates no ambiguity and accepts no division, and the banner becomes a standard of uprightness, not a tool for display; a guide to the right path, not a means of waving. Once the direction is decided, the excuse of hesitation falls away; and once the road is made clear, the fragility of standing in the middle is exposed.

Here language becomes a trust, a decision and a covenant. Speech is asked about its effect just as action is asked about its outcome; silence is held accountable for its position just as speech is held accountable for its intention. Silence is not always wisdom, nor is speech always frivolity; the measure is a stand that is taken, a price that is paid and a covenant that is kept.

Nearness, in this context, is not measured by place but by position, and is not known by slogan but by commitment. Claims fall away layer by layer until the truth remains, stripped of illusions, demanding of its bearer constancy, perseverance and the work that achieves, not the talk that drains.

From here reading turns into action, and the book becomes a field of trial, not a gathering of dreams; a place of duty, not a moment of pleasant harmony. Whoever enters this context enters it knowingly: that clarity strips away the illusion of agreement to establish the reality of what is upright; that honesty in speech exposes crookedness in action; and that calling things by their names is justice, not hostility.

It is a path of standing up that does not evade, and a road of uprightness that does not end: the path of standing in the right place and bearing its consequences with constancy. Whoever finds this station heavy should review himself before he reviews the words; for when the word becomes a covenant it binds, when it becomes a banner it holds to account, and when it becomes nearness it forbids escape.

To the word when it strips off the ornament of illusions, puts on the robe of precision, and stands in the arena of the days fearing neither dispute nor blame; to the word when it is a standing up, not mere talk; a covenant, not melodies; a scale, not dreams. Here it goes out not to delight the ears but to raise the building; not to plant stillness in hearts but to awaken in them daring and courage.

Speech is either a sword that separates truth from dispute and exposes falsehood in the crowd, or an echo that melts into echoes and illusions; either a light that pierces the darkness and establishes what is right, or a smoke that chokes understanding and drowns it in vagueness. There is no glory in a word that decorates without making clear, and no value in a speech that raises its voice without establishing order. A word that is not action is an illusion, and a word that is not a stand is a shadow that melts at the first clash.

Here opposites meet: truth and falsehood, standing and collapse, constancy and division. And here it becomes clear that a stand is what separates the one who speaks and passes like a cloud from the one who speaks and plants landmarks in the earth and sets up pillars and foundations. Truth does not adorn itself to please; it strips itself bare to bind. It does not flatter to make peace; it speaks frankly in order to judge and set the scale upright.

A covenant is not ink that is poured and then dries; it is a fire written in the conscience that sets it upright and rouses it. If it is true, it gives light; if it betrays, it burns and sets up against its owner the court of the days. And the banner is not a piece of cloth raised in the crowd, but a trust carried in places of confrontation and a value upheld in the face of division. Whoever raises it for decoration falls at the first test, and whoever carries it for the truth stands firm, upright and lasting.

When language is stripped of flattery it becomes a mirror of clear precision, showing faces as they truly are, without disguise or darkening, and calling things by their names with the naming of justice, not the naming of illusion. It is either a standing for the truth that is written in the record of the noble, or a bowing to the wind that is folded away in the ledger of defeat.

It is a road that accepts no halfway point and allows no division, that does not tolerate a postponed decision or a promise of easy peace. Clarity on it is a standing up, decisiveness is precision, and honesty is a covenant that is not broken, bargained over or wronged. Whoever enters it enters knowing that comfort is not its aim — meaning is its aim; and that constancy is more lasting than words, heavier than dreams, and truer than every claim made in the crowd.

Here the word is not an echo but a shock that wakes people; not an ornament but an earthquake that raises them up; not a tale to be told but a truth decided in the arena of the days. Whoever speaks it speaks a covenant, whoever carries it carries a trust, and whoever believes it believes in a road that neither swerves nor wanders: a light that, when it shines, removes the shadows, sets up the scale, and steadies the human being in the station of standing upright.

These words are not a conclusion thrown in at the end of the lines and then forgotten, but a covenant cast into the heart of a lifetime and then tended; not a dot extinguished when the speaking ends, but a flame lit when the standing up begins.

Here evasive interpretation falls as masks fall, and the false excuse recedes as shadows recede, and nothing remains but the stand, separating truth from illusion. Either a hearing that passes and cools, or an awareness that settles and endures; either a speech that decorates and seduces, or a speech that clarifies and gives life.

If you are true to the word, it will be true to you; if you deceive it, it will expose you. If you make it a covenant, it will raise you up; if you make it an echo, it will dissolve your commitment. The road is clear and does not bargain, the scale stands and does not flatter, and the truth shines and bows neither to whim nor to fear of conflict.

So choose your station before it is chosen for you, and stand in your place before the wind drags you away and the days fold you up. For here words are not written only to be kept in memory, but to be lived out in life, in a way that is not undone, not erased and not humbled.

intro: In the procession of great lives, among the bright halls of distinction, and in the records of those whose names do not pass like clouds but stand firm as mountains, shine like stars and take root like deep foundations, rises the name of the writer and author Yousef Ahmad Al-Maiari. It stands tall and unbending, and it shines as a great meaning shines when it is joined to virtue, when virtue is crowned by creativity, and when creativity is upheld by knowledge, refined by taste and guarded by dignity.

This is not a man who can be summed up by a single quality, confined to one title or captured in a short phrase. His is a composite character, made of many virtues. Where the sciences are mentioned, he holds a leading place; where the arts are mentioned, he holds a share of mastery. In medicine he gives proof of skill and precision; in literature he shows the brilliance of eloquence and the authority of the pen; in poetry he brings a breath like light travelling through the night; and in art and painting he has the hand of an image-maker who makes colour speak, sets the line free and awakens in the picture a glow of captivating beauty.

In medicine he is not merely a practitioner but a man of sight and insight, of thought and perception. He reads the body not only with the eye of the profession but with the eye of wisdom as well. He reaches the source of illness with an expert’s precision and seeks the paths of healing with a caring hand, uniting the exactness of science with the warmth of humanity, the rigour of diagnosis with sensitivity of feeling, and knowledge of the cause with attention to its effects. His horizon did not narrow before alternative and complementary medicine; it widened to embrace them with the depth of a dedicated researcher. He made of treatment an understanding, of care a kindness, of his profession a covenant, and of his experience a key to a world where the health of the body meets the calm of the soul, and where the wisdom of science embraces human compassion.

In literature he is a true man of letters. When he writes, the phrase shines in his hand like a polished gem; when he shapes a meaning, he dresses it in such beauty of wording and strength of composition that it gains splendour upon splendour and grace upon grace. His words do not fall loosely as they come, nor do they scatter like dry straw; they are strung on a tight thread and set in a measured order, until his prose becomes an architecture of meanings, a procession of forms, a garden of images and a season of significance. Reading him, you feel you are before a pen that does not merely write letters but opens a road for meaning, raises an edifice for ideas and lifts a banner for beauty.

In poetry he is a poet who does not borrow sensitivity; it flows from him. He does not force the glow; it springs from within. When his poetry runs, it runs like streams through a garden; when it glows, it glows like dawn at the edges of night; and when it touches hearts, it touches them as the breeze touches branches, moving them without harshness and filling them without noise. His verse has a tenderness that does not weaken, a strength that is never harsh, a beauty that does not break and a meaning that does not narrow. When he speaks, he does not merely utter words: he plants feelings. He does not just arrange lines: he builds atmospheres. He does not just make images: he paints scenes that stay in the memory long after the reading is done.

In art and painting he is an artist in whose breath colours turn into melodies, lines into echoes, and the canvas from a silent surface into a living being with an eye that sees, a heart that feels and a spirit that soars through the space of form. When he takes up colour, he holds it not as a tool but as a language; when he draws a line, he sends it not as a movement but as a pulse; and when he builds a painting, he builds it not only as a shape but as a vision and a symbol. It is as if in painting he were a poet without words, and in poetry a painter without colours. In both he reaches a depth of effect that turns reception into wonder, wonder into admiration, and admiration into insight.

The great secret of this remarkable character is that it rests neither on a cold collection of talents nor on a silent pile of qualities, but on a fertile harmony in which the faculties are ordered, the paths unite and differences fuse until they become one in appearance and one in essence. For him medicine is not one door, literature another and art a third; they are rivers flowing into one sea, branches rising from one trunk, and lights pouring from one lamp. His knowledge is blended with wisdom, his wisdom shaped by taste, his taste grounded in thought, and his thought adorned with feeling, until his character became a solid structure whose parts support one another, a lofty tower whose summit draws its strength from its base, and a radiant crown in which pearls of every colour and shape are set together.

So his career was never a passing success or a moment of distinction that fades, but a continuous ascent towards a complete form, a gradual building of values, and a steady climb towards peaks that rise and do not dim. He was not content to be successful; he aspired to be unique. He was not satisfied with being accomplished; he sought to be complete. He did not settle for having talent; he made it his aim to have a whole character, in which talent and profession are brothers, knowledge and inspiration embrace, thought and image intertwine, and work and beauty become one, until the self becomes a great unity with no division in its parts, no weakness in its joints and no disorder in its structure. He is, in short, not just a name to be written but a horizon to contemplate; not just a life to be told but a painting with gilded edges, bright colours and deep shadows; not just a man who combined different arts but one who made harmony from their differences and order from their diversity. His life shows that a person of high resolve, pure taste, broad mind and steady effort can unite the majesty of science with the beauty of art, the precision of craft with the splendour of the image, and the dignity of standing with the sweetness of lasting influence.

A figure of this stature deserves to have its story written in the ink of reverence, not in the passing ink of description, and to be told in a style worthy of it, not in words that fall short. For this is a character that is not simply mentioned and praised: it is cited as an example of completeness and held up as evidence of true talent. In it one sees how a person can rise from the limits of a specialty to a broad purpose, from mere success to a lasting legacy, and from excellence to uniqueness.

The writer and author Yousef Ahmad Al-Maiari is a towering figure: where knowledge is present, he brings its dignity; where literature is present, its splendour; where poetry is present, its radiance; and where art is present, its magic. Taken as a whole, his is a character crowned by knowledge, adorned with talent, grounded in experience and clothed in dignity. If it can be said of some people that they are repeated copies of the ordinary, then the truth about this man is that he is of a rare and fine kind: a beautiful weave, a shining example, a noble metal, a precious gem, a generous character, an upright path, a sound method, a lasting influence and a fragrant memory. His equal is rare, his worth undiminished, and his name does not pass by as passers-by do.

p: The academic and scientific training of the writer and author Yousef Ahmad Al-Maiari rests on a solid foundation of structured study, multiple specialisations and a breadth of knowledge spanning health and therapy, management and development. His academic path is the picture of continuous effort, cumulative learning and a vision that does not stop at the borders of a single field.

He earned a doctorate in public health, combined with a specialisation in complementary natural medicine and herbal medicine. He holds the title of professor of natural herbal medicine and earned a second doctorate in the philosophy of natural therapy, reflecting his deep interest in the theoretical and practical foundations of treatment and his effort to connect medical knowledge with its philosophical horizon.

In management and human development his training broadened remarkably: he earned a doctorate in business administration and human resources and a research master’s degree in human development, as well as diplomas in human resources and development, in “triple power”, and in human energy. Together these give him a training that joins management in its organisational sense with development in its human sense, showing a wide horizon and a varied set of tools.

His qualifications did not remain theoretical. He has taken on professional, advisory and development roles, working as a family counsellor and a mental health specialist, as a legal adviser, and as a trainer of trainers in management consulting and human resources. This highlights the practical side of his work and shows that his experience was never confined to lecture halls and certificates, but extended into practice, service and real influence.

This academic and scientific training is therefore not only a list of qualifications. It reveals a person who made learning a path, knowledge a structure, and specialisation a bridge to a broader understanding of people: their health, their management, their awareness, their energy and their capacity to grow and rise.

The writer and author Yousef Ahmad Al-Maiari is known for his specialisation in treating cancer and chronic diseases, combining modern medical methods with the long-established principles of alternative medicine and traditional herbal therapy. He founded a medical centre for research and studies in Ukraine, which provides consultations and treatment for complex conditions including cancer, multiple sclerosis, diabetes and neurological diseases.
He also received the gold medal in reproductive medicine and is a member of a number of respected international academic organisations and bodies, including:

Combining scholarly rigour with elevated thought, he has made his voice heard at conferences, defending justice and dignity and building bridges of dialogue between peoples. His experience embodies the global thinker whom borders do not confine and who contributes to the awareness of humanity.

cards.p: He speaks five languages fluently: Arabic, Russian, Ukrainian, German and Italian.

Alongside his medicine and his writing, he is a visual artist and an athlete. He uses painting and sport together to strengthen focus and build inner balance, combining physical strength with artistic imagination, and disciplined movement with sensitivity of feeling.

end: This rich career shows that Yousef Ahmad Al-Maiari has made science more than food for the mind and art more than an ornament for the soul: he has made them two wings on which a person can rise towards creativity and reform, meaning and lasting impact. For him, joining medicine and thought, the pen and the brush, is neither a luxury nor a pastime, but a covenant of the spirit and the conviction of a soul that chose to unite the light of insight with the beauty of the image, the majesty of truth with the grace of expression. In his hands science softens without losing its firmness, and art finds order without losing its life, until the two meet in one harmony where precision is reconciled with beauty and reason with taste. His mind stays bright, his heart sensitive, his influence lasting and his memory ever renewed. His life then becomes not a story to be told but an example to follow; not words to be spoken but a value that gives life meaning, a vision that awakens awareness, and proof that a person who builds himself honestly can turn his knowledge into mercy, his art into wisdom and his life into a legacy that endures.

p: The value of reading is not measured by the number of pages we turn, but by the depth of the meanings we understand, the accuracy of the knowledge we gain and the soundness of the judgements we build. I have read these books in full, reflected on the knowledge, methods and experience they contain, and been influenced by much of what I found in them: careful research, breadth of view, beauty of expression and a deep portrayal of people and life.

But reading something does not mean endorsing it, and being influenced does not mean adopting it. Not everything that is read is accepted, and not everything that is beautifully worded is true. Listing these books is not an endorsement of all their contents, nor agreement with every word, opinion or idea in them. Whatever contradicts my faith and my principles I reject and do not follow: the fame of a speaker does not make his words true, and elegant phrasing does not make an error right.

This is my approach to reading Arabic and foreign books alike. I stress in particular that benefiting from foreign books does not mean accepting anything in them that contradicts our faith, our values and our good customs and traditions. Knowing an opinion is one thing; adopting it is another.

I read to understand and to discern, to benefit from what is right, to set aside what is wrong, and to grow in knowledge while staying true to my principles. Knowledge comes through learning, and thoughtful reading is one of its means; but reading alone is not enough to master a field or become qualified in it. Some of my reading is for study and learning, and some is for enjoyment and widening my horizons. Real mastery of a subject requires structured learning, careful understanding, patient review and turning to specialists where things are unclear. What counts is sound understanding, not the quantity of quotations; mastery of knowledge, not the number of books.

Diagnosis comes before the prescription, and evidence governs treatment: guesswork does not replace examination, nor claims replace proof.
A remedy’s popularity does not prove that it works, and coming from a natural source does not guarantee that it is safe.
The patient’s safety and dignity are a trust, and his interest comes before any gain: his need is not exploited, and his rights are not violated.
Every patient has his own condition, and every treatment its own rules: remedies are not applied to everyone alike, and individual differences are not overlooked.
Honesty requires stating the limits of treatment: no benefit is exaggerated, no harm is concealed, and no cure is guaranteed.

blocks: I chose herbal medicine because I found in the world of plants something that rouses my mind and draws my heart: in the green of a leaf there is the story of a life, and in a root reaching deep into the soil there is an image of patience and growth. Yet this beauty opens a door to contemplation for me; it is not, on its own, proof that a remedy works. Knowledge has its evidence, responsibility has its scales, and human health has a sanctity that governs every judgement.

My choice was not a mere fondness for the old, nor an infatuation with everything green the earth puts forth. It was a longing for a kind of care that sees the human being whole: a body in pain, a mind that worries, a heart that hopes. A patient is not a symptom reduced to a line, nor a number entered in a register. A patient is a person carrying both pain and hope, who places their trust in my hands; and that trust becomes a duty that demands honest words, careful observation and good care.

When I call this approach “authentic medicine”, I mean authenticity of care, purity of intention, and a firm bond between knowledge and compassion. For me, authenticity is a responsibility to be carried, knowledge to be examined, and a trust to be honoured. What we have inherited from those before us deserves respect accompanied by verification, and appreciation joined with scrutiny: we keep what is sound, clarify what is uncertain and set aside what has been shown to be wrong, with a mind that checks, a conscience that is fair, and an insight not clouded by partisanship.

I want this authenticity to show in my conduct before my words: in a question I ask with care, a complaint I listen to with patience, and a decision I make with deliberation. A name cannot grant its bearer a virtue he has not earned through his work, and belonging to a school of treatment does not exempt anyone from accountability. The worth of an approach shows in sound practice, in respect for patients’ rights and in good care; through these, words ring true and trust takes root.

I have chosen to place faithfulness to my duty above the wish to persuade, and to let my concern for the patient be stronger than my eagerness to prove my point. What is eloquence worth if it hides a lack of knowledge? What honour is there in a remedy surrounded by promises no evidence supports? Reassurance that conceals the truth may give a patient a moment’s comfort, then burden them with consequences they had every right to know and I had every duty to explain.

I want the knowledge in my work to rise through precision, and my self-confidence to be tempered by humility. Knowledge is not measured by how many names we memorise or how unusual the terms we use; it shows in sound understanding, sound judgement and a careful distinction between what we know and what we merely suppose. The words “I do not know”, said in their proper place, can be a truer sign of integrity than an eloquent answer that dresses ignorance in fine language.

There is a tangible beauty in plants that captivates me: a rising scent, an opening leaf, a seed waking in the stillness of the soil. But the senses that perceive this beauty are not enough to judge whether a plant is fit to treat. Here the question comes before admiration, and inclination submits to evidence: what benefit of this plant has been established? What are the cautions in using it? For whom is it suitable? And when is declining to prescribe it the more knowledgeable, the more caring and the more faithful choice?

When I consider prescribing a herb, I make sure of its identity and quality, its dose and the limits of its use, and any medicines it may interact with. I find out what I need to know about the patient to judge whether it suits them; a prescription is a trust concerning a person with their own circumstances, needs and medical history, all of which call for care and attention to detail. Harm can lie in a small detail we overlooked or a necessary question we failed to ask, so keeping a patient safe begins with asking well, before we ever reach the stage of prescribing.

That is why I do not say that everything the earth grows is safe, nor that everything people make is harmful. Fairness keeps me from generalising ahead of the evidence, and integrity makes me verify before I judge. What I seek is a treatment whose expected benefits outweigh its risks in the particular case, and whose limits and cautions are clear. My love of plants makes me all the more careful about the truth of what I attribute to them: every therapeutic claim needs evidence to support it, and every benefit mentioned must be stated within the limits of what has been established.

It pains me when human suffering becomes an opportunity for exploitation, when a practitioner’s success is measured by how much he sells, and when a patient’s fear for their health is used to draw out their money. So I reject every trade that feeds on people’s pain, whether in the clinic or in the herb shop. Greed is good at hiding in many guises; integrity is revealed when personal gain conflicts with duty. That is where conscience is tested and true integrity shows itself.

I want patients to understand their condition better, to be more aware of their options and more able to share in decisions about their treatment. I do not count frequent return visits, in themselves, as a sign of success; success may show instead in an improved condition, a clear treatment plan and freedom from what the patient does not need. I see preserving their dignity as a duty at every stage of care, from the first question to the last instruction, so that their voice is heard, their rights are protected and their decisions rest on understanding.

I refuse to let a patient’s body become a field for irresponsible improvisation or a means of building false fame. I distinguish such recklessness from disciplined scientific research, which is governed by oversight and ethical standards and requires informed consent. Patients have the right to know the nature of what is proposed to them, the benefit hoped for, and the risks and uncertainties around it, before they give their consent, so that it is consent lit by knowledge, protected by awareness and given freely.

True concern for the patient shows when their interest conflicts with my pride in my own opinion; that is where integrity is tested and sincerity of purpose becomes clear. If a patient needs a test, I direct them to it; if they need a specialist, I refer them; and if their condition calls for urgent intervention, I do not let my convictions become an obstacle that delays the care they need. I did not choose plants to narrow my horizons; I chose them as a field of knowledge and service, and the patient’s interest deserves more care than my wish to win an argument.

Nor do I think it right to move a person from one dogma to another, or to destroy their trust in every medicine in order to build their trust in my remedy. Trust raised by exaggeration is shaken when the truth comes out, while reassurance grounded in honesty helps a person choose well. I want my words to give the patient the insight to know the limits and cautions of a treatment, and to understand that changing or stopping a prescribed treatment requires a responsible medical review that takes their condition into account and keeps them safe.

My love of plant-based treatment obliges me to be all the more rigorous. A true lover protects what he loves from claims that have no evidence behind them, and shields it from exaggeration that lifts it up for an hour and then lets it fall for a long time. One benefit established by evidence and stated within its limits is worth more than stories so woven with promises that they bury the truth. Knowledge grows through precision, gains strength through review and proves its soundness when it submits to questioning and scrutiny.

I like treatment to be a dialogue with plenty of room for listening, in which the patient hears an explanation they can understand, asks questions without embarrassment and disagrees without fear. The respect I hope for comes from clear knowledge, steady character and honest dealings. Patience with a patient’s questions is respect for their mind; explaining the limits of treatment protects their trust; listening to their fears honours their rights. In this way they find in their care knowledge to guide them, kindness to comfort them and integrity to protect their dignity.

As I picture this path, knowledge is light, compassion is warmth, and conscience is the scales. When light is cut off from warmth, knowledge turns cold; when warmth is cut off from light, emotion turns blind; and when the scales are missing, judgement goes astray. I seek to bring these together in my work: a mind that verifies, a heart that is gentle, a tongue that is truthful, and a hand that finds where to intervene and knows when holding back is wiser and more right.

The market may want a glittering phrase; I want an honest word. People may be eager for a promise; I believe that patience is sometimes the truest form of compassion. I do not promise what knowledge does not support, and I do not close the window of hope where there is evidence for it. I set out clearly what I know, I explain the limits of what I know, and I protect the patient’s right to choose. I review my judgements and hold myself to account, so that my words stay within my knowledge and my work within my integrity.

That is why I chose herbal medicine: a field in which I serve people with the benefits of herbs that have been established, while respecting their cautions, and in which I keep the compassionate face of care. I want my authenticity to be known by my integrity, my knowledge to show in my precision, and my care for the patient to appear in the protection of their rights and dignity. If holding to my convictions ever conflicts with the patient’s safety, I put their safety first and reconsider my convictions. This is the authenticity of medicine as I understand it, and its trust as I hope to fulfil it.
why.q: Why did you choose herbal medicine, and why do you call it “authentic medicine” rather than “alternative medicine”?

blocks: Healing with plants and herbs is one of the oldest paths of treatment humanity has known. Many societies have relied on it across the ages, and it has held a central place in their medical knowledge and healing practice. Centuries before pharmaceutical factories and advanced diagnostic equipment appeared, medicinal plants already had precise names, known uses and books devoted to describing them and setting out their properties. Plant medicine thus became an essential part of the history of medicine, and a field that deserves study and a fair hearing.

In this article we call it “authentic medicine”, in recognition of its deep roots and its contribution to the lives of nations. When some modern contexts call it “alternative medicine”, that name describes its position in a particular setting; it does not erase its place in history. Every term has its context, and knowledge has its continuity.

I believe the roots of this medicine reach back to the time of Adam, peace be upon him, and that knowledge of healing with plants and herbs, including what later became part of Arab medicine, goes back to a revelation that God, blessed and exalted, gave him. God granted him knowledge and taught him the properties of plants, the benefits of herbs and the ways of healing with them, so that he knew what helps and what harms, what is used against disease and what holds the hope of a cure. He then taught his children what he had learned and passed on to them what he had mastered, and they inherited this knowledge generation after generation, until its legacy reached us.

The passing on of healing knowledge widened over time, spreading from families to circles of learning and fields of practice. Each generation carried what it had received, added what it had learned and handed it on to those who came after. In this way experience crossed the borders of villages and countries; then writing preserved much of this knowledge and made it material for reading, comparison and review, after part of it had been kept only in memory and passed on through practice.

From the perspective of faith, God, blessed and exalted, is the Creator of plants and of the properties within them, and the Giver of the human mind and the means of knowledge. Part of being grateful for these blessings is to study the benefits of plants, to know the cautions in using them and to make good use of them. Caring for plants brings together reflection on the wonder of creation, eagerness to benefit people, and responsibility in using what God has placed at humanity’s service.

The great works on medicines did not come about by chance. Behind them lay collecting and tracing, travel and inquiry, observation and comparison. Their authors paid close attention to the names of plants and their different names, where they grow and the species that resemble them; for a remedy needs a known substance, and a substance needs a definition that sets it apart. This is where the value of description, naming and classification lies: they fix knowledge in place and bring it within reach of those who seek it.

Islamic and Arab civilisation made a notable contribution to this field. It produced books on single remedies, others on compounds and prescriptions, and works combining both. The variety of environments and the reach of travel helped in identifying many medicinal substances, and the exchange of knowledge enriched what was written. These efforts reveal a concern for ordering knowledge and an awareness of the value of books in preserving experience and making it easy to consult.

Among the finest witnesses to this heritage are pharmacological works written centuries ago, in which their authors gathered knowledge of medicines and foods, drawing on their own observations and on earlier works. These works testify to the long-standing care for this field in Islamic and Arab civilisation, and to successive efforts to gather its knowledge, order its questions and pass its experience from one generation to the next.

The importance of these works shows in the breadth of pharmacological knowledge they display and in how long ago it was organised: behind every book stand other books, and behind every author stand generations of researchers and healers. The wealth of their material and the variety of their sources show how long this science has been cultivated, and reveal a heritage built by successive efforts, one that deserves a reading that grasps its depth and a study that edits it well. By comparison, the essential features of modern medicine took shape over the last two centuries, roughly 180 years ago. This dating shows how many centuries of writing on medicines and work with medicinal plants came before that stage.

What is authentically reported from our master Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, on healing deserves reverence and care: its transmission should be verified, its meaning established and its understanding referred to scholars, with knowledge of the conditions for applying it. Knowledge is a trust in how it is transmitted, interpreted and acted upon, and that responsibility grows when it concerns a person’s health and their hope of recovery.

Plant medicine is a field that requires solid training. Knowing the name of a herb is only a beginning, to be followed by knowing its species, the part used, how it is prepared, its dose and the cautions in using it. Some herbal preparations can interact with medicines, and their safety depends on the quality of preparation and the purity of the material. Precision in knowing and using herbs is therefore at the core of a practitioner’s responsibility to the patient.

The trustworthy practitioner in this field is careful with his promises, makes sure his information is accurate and puts the patient’s interest before his own fame and profit. The higher the standard of education, documentation and quality control, the greater the trust in disciplined practice. The practitioner owes mastery; the patient is owed honesty and care; and through both the dignity of the profession is preserved and its purpose kept true.

What we owe authentic medicine is to turn our interest in it into action: editing its books, studying its plants, preserving its resources and training those who work in it. This calls for well-made indexes, serious education programmes and research that defines where it helps and where its use ends. The roots deserve to be preserved, the knowledge deserves to be verified, and people deserve to benefit; in this way faithfulness is kept, authenticity protected and the giving renewed.

Commentators on scripture have noted that medicine was prominent in the time of Jesus, peace be upon him, and that its practitioners were skilled in healing by the knowledge of their age. His miracle therefore came in what their craft could not achieve: he healed, by God’s permission, the man born blind and the leper. This was not superior skill in compounding a remedy but a miracle that showed the truth of his prophethood and revealed the limits of human ability. It also shows the standing medicine had at that time.

In our own time, health institutions acknowledge the contribution of plants to the discovery of important medicines: some have an active substance extracted from a plant, and others were developed from plant compounds. However far machines advance and formulations are refined, this does not erase the plant origin of these medicines, nor cancel its value in research and discovery.

This authentic medicine is not attained by wishing, nor is the right to practise it inherited. A person may inherit books and recipes, but not the understanding and mastery that go with them. Mastery comes through disciplined learning, training under qualified supervision and constant review of one’s knowledge. Lineage does not take the place of study, fame does not replace competence, and good intentions are not enough to protect a patient’s health. The profession is a responsibility that comes before the title, and knowledge is an effort that comes before practice. Whoever wishes to benefit people must know the extent of his knowledge and the limits of his specialism, and not go beyond them.

blocks: Irritable bowel syndrome is a common disorder of the digestive system. Its symptoms include recurring abdominal pain, bloating and a change in bowel habits, with diarrhoea or constipation, which may alternate in some people. These symptoms are affected by many factors, including diet, lifestyle and psychological stress, so caring for them starts with understanding what the body needs and choosing what suits it.

Caring for irritable bowel syndrome combines the benefit of suitable food, regular daily habits and the use of certain appropriate plant preparations. These are chosen according to the main symptom, whether pain, bloating or constipation; what relieves one person may differ from what relieves another.

Peppermint comes first among the plants studied for relieving the symptoms of irritable bowel syndrome, as its oil helps relax the smooth muscle of the intestines. Studies point to the benefit of enteric-coated peppermint oil capsules in easing abdominal pain and some other symptoms in adults in the short term.

Ginger is one of the best-known plants used for digestion, and its benefit stands out in easing some kinds of nausea. Chamomile, fennel and sage appear in the traditional use of herbal drinks for digestive comfort: chamomile for relaxation and for calming digestive discomfort, fennel for wind and bloating, and sage for some complaints of indigestion. These drinks are chosen according to the person’s comfort and how they respond.

Flaxseed contains fibre and beneficial fatty acids, and may help soften stools and regulate bowel movements, especially for those prone to constipation. It is added to the diet gradually, with regular water intake, so that its effect is gentler on the gut.

Soluble fibre plays an important part in regulating bowel movements and easing the symptoms of irritable bowel syndrome. Its sources include oats and psyllium husk, and the amount is increased gradually according to tolerance and need. Carrots and sweet potatoes can also form part, in suitable amounts, of a balanced diet that provides fibre, vitamins and minerals.

Fruit and vegetables add variety to the diet and supply the body with useful nutrients, and people with the condition benefit most when they choose the kinds and amounts they tolerate. Apples and mangoes, for all their nutritional value, can trigger symptoms in some people, so the choice depends on individual response.

Some kinds of yoghurt and kefir contain live microorganisms, and some probiotics may help ease symptoms in some people. The benefit depends on the product and on how the body responds, choosing lactose-free products where needed. Some people with the condition can tolerate cheeses that are low in lactose.

Low-fat chicken and turkey are a source of protein, best prepared in light ways such as boiling or grilling, with care in choosing additions the person tolerates. The same attention to fat content and cooking method applies to other meats.

Ways of easing symptoms include eating fewer rich and fried meals, and limiting coffee, tea and fizzy drinks when they are linked to digestive complaints. The effect of alcoholic drinks and of some sweeteners found in sugar-free products should also be considered, as they may increase wind or diarrhoea.

Cutting down for a limited period on foods rich in fermentable carbohydrates, such as onions, garlic and some fruits, may help. Foods are then reintroduced gradually to find the suitable kinds and amounts, balancing gut comfort with a varied diet.

This care is completed by regular meals, eating slowly, drinking water regularly, getting enough sleep, and walking or doing suitable physical activity. Keeping a record of foods and symptoms helps show what suits the body, and relaxation and well-planned rest help reduce the effect of stress. When herbs are used alongside other medicines, the treating doctor should be consulted to choose what suits the condition.

Caring for irritable bowel syndrome rests on good choices, regularity and follow-up. Suitable food, considered use of plant preparations and balanced daily habits work together to reduce suffering and improve quality of life. The better people understand their condition and watch how they respond, the better able they are to build a routine that brings comfort and keeps their diet balanced.
ibs.q: In our conversation with Dr. Yousef Al-Maiari about one of the most common health problems affecting many people’s lives, we asked him, as a researcher in alternative and plant medicine, about the benefits of herbs and foods for irritable bowel syndrome. He replied:

blocks: Not everything that helps one person helps another, and not everything popular among people suits every case. This is where proper care of the body begins: understanding what it needs before choosing a food or a remedy for it. Knowledge comes before treatment, qualification comes before practice, and the aim of treatment is to benefit the person and ease their suffering.

Many people know the names of herbs and pass their recipes around, yet they may not know the cause of their own symptoms, or whether those recipes suit them. Someone hears that a herb helped a relative and assumes it will help them just as much. In reality, similar complaints do not mean the same cause, and a suitable plan takes into account the patient’s condition, circumstances and needs.

Medical heritage knew the theory of the four humours: blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile. Ancient physicians believed that keeping them in balance preserved health and that an imbalance led to disease. This idea formed an important part of their language for describing bodies, explaining symptoms and choosing foods and medicines, and so it was present in their books, their teaching and their practice.

In this traditional classification, blood was said to be hot and moist, phlegm cold and moist, yellow bile hot and dry, and black bile cold and dry. These descriptions belonged to a theory that linked the humours to the four qualities of heat, cold, moisture and dryness, so they should be understood in their historical and technical context.

“Temperament” in this terminology is broader than a passing mood: it does not simply mean happiness or anger, but what they believed resulted from the mixing of those qualities in the body. On this basis they described foods and medicines as hot or cold, and tried to choose what they thought suited the patient’s temperament and condition.

One of the subtleties of studying this heritage is that calling a food hot or cold did not always refer to its temperature when eaten, but to the effect they attributed to it in the body according to their theory. Disciplined learning helps distinguish these meanings and prevents confusing the traditional term with a direct physical description.

Studying these terms helps us understand the history of medicine and the methods of its practitioners. In present-day treatment, however, humoral theory is not an accepted scientific basis for diagnosing disease or deciding treatment. Respecting heritage means understanding it well; caring for the patient requires scientific and practical training, and reliance on examination, evidence and proper assessment.

It is not enough for someone who feels cold to conclude that phlegm dominates them, for someone often angry to blame yellow bile, or for someone who is sad to take black bile as the explanation. Such isolated observations do not make a diagnosis. It is more useful to describe one’s symptoms accurately and to seek an understanding of their causes by consulting a trusted doctor.

Careful observation helps people know their bodies: noticing when a complaint appears, how long it lasts, how it relates to food, sleep and activity, and what medicines or preparations they are taking. It helps to write this down in a short note to show a trusted doctor; a written record makes the sequence of symptoms clear and helps in assessing the response to treatment.

Observation has value when it is understood in context. Improvement after taking something does not by itself prove that it caused the improvement. Symptoms may change over time, or with changes in diet and rest. This is where the specialist’s role appears: interpreting and connecting the information, distinguishing coincidence from cause, and judging what needs follow-up.

blocks.h: Knowing the herb and its preparation

blocks: In authentic medicine, meaning herbal medicine in this discussion, knowledge begins with identifying the plant correctly and knowing the part used, how it is prepared and the purpose of using it. The part used may be the leaf, seed or root, and the preparation may be an infusion, an extract or capsules; these differences are studied and taken into account when choosing.

Knowledge of herbs does not rest on memorising their names alone. The dose, the length of use, the quality of the preparation and its suitability for the patient are all part of that knowledge. A light infusion can differ from a concentrated extract so much that different guidance is needed. Judging these matters requires organised learning, practical training and, when needed, consultation with a trusted doctor.

A practical example is enteric-coated peppermint oil capsules. They have been studied for easing some symptoms of irritable bowel syndrome in adults and have shown benefit for some of them in the short term. What is meant here is a specific preparation for a specific condition, chosen after consulting a trusted doctor, with its result followed according to how the symptoms improve and how well it suits the person.

This example shows that the use of a plant becomes more precise when it is linked to a studied preparation and a known purpose. The results for the capsules do not automatically apply to peppermint tea, and the same benefit should not be assumed for every digestive complaint. This precision is one of the fruits of learning, which sharpens discernment and puts information in its proper place.

When starting any treatment advice, it helps the patient to ask about the expected goal, the right length of time to judge the result, and what would call for another review. These questions make them an informed partner in caring for their health and help them stick to a plan whose purpose they understand and whose effect they follow.

The principle of suitability applies to food as well: the type of food, its amount and how it is prepared are taken into account, and its effect is understood in the light of the person’s condition. It is wise for dietary changes to be clear and gradual, and to avoid broad restrictions without need. The aim is comfort while keeping the diet varied, sufficient and practical for daily life.

When herbs are used alongside other medicines, a trusted doctor must be consulted and told the names and amounts of the preparations. This matters even more with a chronic illness, during pregnancy and breastfeeding, or when treating children. Such a review helps coordinate treatment and choose what is suitable, while continuing the prescribed treatment unless the doctor decides to change it.

The trustworthy practitioner of herbal medicine combines study with training, knows the limits of his specialism and refers a case to someone better able to assess it when needed. Experience is refined through study and supervised practice, knowledge grows through continued learning, and trust is built on honesty and mastery. A practitioner’s fame does not replace his qualifications, just as the popularity of a recipe does not replace verifying it.

A person may inherit books, recipes and stories of the experience of those before him; these are material for study and research. The right to treat, however, is earned through learning, training and assessment, and is not passed down by lineage. A learner’s standing shows in the precision of his understanding, the soundness of his practice, his good judgement and his honesty about what he knows and what he still needs to learn.

No one becomes a doctor merely by reading. Reading is one of the means of learning; a doctor’s qualification is the fruit of specialised education, clinical training under qualified supervision and an assessment of competence. Learning the properties of a herb, or one branch of healing, does not replace this qualification, nor does it give anyone the right to diagnose and treat every disease.

Teaching is a responsibility that goes hand in hand with learning. Whoever undertakes to teach others must master what he teaches, explain its limits, and train his students to ask, to verify and to be honest. It is not enough for a student to memorise a recipe; he must learn when it suits a case, how it is used, how its result is followed, and when the patient needs to be referred.

The learner has a right to teaching that distinguishes inherited use from studied results, and personal experience from evidence that can be relied on. Saying that a plant was used in the past describes its history; proving its therapeutic benefit requires evidence to support it. With this distinction, teaching stays sound, practice stays disciplined, and the student learns to weigh every piece of information by the strength of its evidence.

Faithfulness to medical heritage lies in studying and verifying it, and kindness to the patient lies in knowledge, competence and good treatment. Whoever wishes to practise medicine should learn in an organised way, train under guidance and complete the requirements of qualification before taking on treatment. Knowledge is a trust, teaching is a responsibility, and human health deserves sound knowledge and a qualified hand.
akhlat.h: The Four Humours and Herbal Medicine: Learning and Qualification Before Practice
akhlat.by: Prepared by Dr. Yousef Ahmad Al-Maiari

blocks: Cupping has a place in the heritage of healing, a firm presence in the Prophetic Sunnah, and a link to people’s efforts to ease their pain and care for their health. Speaking about it calls for an account that combines respect for its standing with accuracy in describing it, and good intentions with skilled practice. Human health is a trust and managing its treatment is a responsibility; any means from which benefit is hoped becomes more valuable when it is used in its proper place and surrounded by knowledge, care and attention to safety.

It is authentically reported that the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, was cupped and said: “The best of what you treat yourselves with is cupping and the sea costus.” This is Prophetic praise that shows its merit as a means of healing and gives it its place in Islamic awareness. “The best” here means the most excellent and most beneficial. Caring for this guidance requires understanding it, applying it well and taking into account the condition of the person seeking treatment, so that respect for the text and concern for the patient come together in one aim: seeking benefit and protecting life.

blocks.h: What kind of cupping is meant?

blocks: The cupping meant in this article is wet cupping, which uses special cups to create local suction, together with limited superficial incisions that allow a quantity of blood to come out. Described in this way, it is a procedure that affects the skin and small blood vessels and requires knowledge, skill and discipline. Understanding its nature helps in judging the care it needs: every procedure that breaks the skin requires precautions to prevent infection and protect the patient from complications.

blocks.h: The doctor decides; the cupping practitioner carries it out

blocks: Including cupping in a treatment plan is preceded by the doctor’s examination and assessment of the patient’s condition, and by deciding whether it suits them and what benefit is hoped for. In this approach, the doctor decides where the cups go according to the medical assessment, and a qualified practitioner carries out the procedure under the doctor’s instructions. The practitioner does not place the cups wherever he sees fit, nor does he diagnose the illness or decide its treatment on his own. In this way the benefit takes on a clear meaning that can be assessed, and the decision to continue or reconsider rests on the doctor’s assessment and the patient’s response, taking into account any other treatments they are receiving. Good treatment combines hope of benefit, careful judgement and faithful execution.

Drawing blood is carried out by a qualified cupping practitioner after the doctor has examined the patient and assessed their condition. The doctor decides whether cupping suits them and sets the sites and limits of the procedure; the qualified practitioner carries it out according to the doctor’s instructions. For the patient’s safety, a practitioner may not cup anyone without first consulting the doctor, who must examine the patient and decide that cupping suits their condition; the practitioner may not make this decision, or choose the cupping sites, on his own. The procedure is done with limited superficial incisions and sterile instruments, while watching the patient’s condition and the bleeding and caring for the site. This is a professional responsibility that cannot be met by random imitation or by watching a video clip. Skill shows in careful execution and attention to the case, in being able to stop when needed, in handling any complication correctly, and in calling for medical help when necessary.

Sterilisation and infection control are fundamental in cupping. Sterile, single-use cutting instruments are used, hands are cleaned and the skin disinfected, and suitable protective equipment is worn. Sharp instruments and contaminated waste are disposed of safely, and single-use instruments are never reused. These measures protect both the patient and the practitioner, because instruments contaminated with blood can transmit infection. Anyone seeking treatment has the right to be assured that these measures are properly applied.

Some conditions call for special caution, including anaemia and bleeding disorders, and chronic illnesses and pregnancy require a medical assessment beforehand. The doctor and the practitioner should be told about any medicines the patient takes, especially blood thinners, and no prescribed medicine should be stopped or its dose changed without consulting the treating doctor. Real care includes knowing when the procedure is appropriate and when it should be avoided, and this is for the doctor to decide after examination and assessment. Concern for the patient means putting their safety before the wish to finish the session, and making a decision that suits their health.

As for timing, cupping may be done when there is a medical need, at a suitable time; there is no need to wait for a particular day of the month. The point is that meeting a need should not be tied to a set date, while respecting the conditions of safety and the patient’s state. Narrations have come down about choosing the 17th, 19th and 21st days of the lunar month, and a number of scholars considered it preferable to be cupped on these days.

Whoever follows this preference, and for whom cupping is suitable, may choose those days, knowing that keeping to them is not a condition for cupping to be permissible, and that a medical need is not postponed to wait for them. When speaking about the Sunnah, it is good to take into account the degrees of authenticity of reports and to mention differences of opinion where they affect understanding. In this way eagerness to follow the Prophetic example goes together with accuracy in transmission, and seeking treatment stays tied to the person’s need and what suits their condition.

Care is completed by follow-up after cupping, watching the state of the skin and how the body responds. Continued bleeding, severe pain, fever, increasing redness and any discharge are all signs that call for a medical assessment. Repeating sessions should therefore be a considered decision, and follow-up should be an opportunity to assess the benefit and catch any problem early. A well-done procedure is preceded by care, accompanied by vigilance and followed by follow-up.

Cupping deserves a fair account that preserves its standing, makes knowledge the guide to its practice and the person’s safety its aim. It is honoured through truthful description, sound choice, skilled work and respect for patients’ rights. Let good intentions and disciplined experience come together, and let eagerness to follow the Prophetic guidance be joined with eagerness to benefit. In this way care is sound, trust takes root, the medical word stays faithful to its trust, and the person remains honoured in dignity, protected in health and treated with gentleness and care.

blocks.h: A word to the cupping practitioner

blocks: You who perform cupping: fear God in the care of those who entrust you with their health, and know that mastering the procedure does not mean mastering diagnosis, and that much practice does not replace the doctor’s examination and assessment. Do not perform cupping before consulting the doctor and making sure it suits the case, and do not place the cups on the strength of judgement that goes beyond your qualifications. A patient’s trust in you is a duty that obliges you to take care, not permission to take risks. Beware of letting past success make you careless with a new case: every patient has their own condition, and every condition its own assessment. Follow the doctor’s instructions and stay within the limits of your knowledge; competence lies not in daring but in sound decisions and honest work. And remember: good intentions do not prevent the harm of haste, and the patient’s safety comes before finishing the session.
hijama.h: Cupping (Hijama): Prophetic Guidance and a Trust in Healing
hijama.by: As stated by Dr. Yousef Ahmad Al-Maiari

blocks: Plants have a firm place in the history of healing. From their roots, leaves and seeds, knowledge took shape, experience accumulated and questions arose that people carried from experience into study. Among these plants stands Indian costus (qust hindi), carrying a long history of use and attracting interest for the compounds it contains and the fields of research it opens.

The value of a plant lies not in how much is said about it, but in how accurately it is known. Knowledge turns fame into a question, the question into research, and research into an understanding that guides practice well. In this way costus takes its place in the discussion of authentic medicine: a plant whose properties are studied, whose benefits are investigated and whose use is regulated.

Indian costus is a perennial herb whose roots are well known in traditional medical systems in Asia. What is sold as “costus wood” is usually pieces of its dried root. Identifying the plant and the part used is the foundation on which the study of its properties is built: accurate identification is the first step to accurate knowledge.

Costus has been used in traditional healing for digestive, respiratory and skin complaints, and the ways of preparing it have varied between environments and medical schools. This long history is rich material for study: inherited experience raises its questions, and organised knowledge tests the answers, until it becomes clear where the benefit lies and what the conditions are for using it.

Costus roots contain many plant compounds, including components of the essential oil and other biologically active compounds. Researchers have studied some of its extracts and components in areas related to inflammation, oxidation and microbes. This research helps in understanding its biological activity and prepares the way for assessing whether therapeutic preparations could be developed from it.

Research has levels that complete one another: a laboratory result reveals possible activity, animal experiments help explain some mechanisms, and clinical studies test benefit and safety in people. Recognising these levels gives each result its proper weight, so that a research promise remains a promise still to be fulfilled, and a proven benefit remains tied to its evidence.

blocks.h: Common uses weighed against the evidence

blocks: On intestinal worms, there are studies on the use of costus roots against certain parasites. Their importance lies in specifying the type of parasite, the preparation used, the dose and the result of treatment. A finding about roots prepared in a particular way does not automatically apply to every oil sold under the name of costus; each preparation has its own composition and its own way of being assessed.

As for the respiratory system, costus has a place in uses related to it, which has encouraged the study of some of its properties. The account is more precise when it links a possible benefit to a specific symptom or condition; lung health covers many functions and diseases, and defining what is meant clarifies both the subject of the study and the patient’s need.

Some people speak of “strengthening the blood” or “activating the blood”. Both phrases need defining: is anaemia meant, or fatigue, or some other complaint? The answer becomes clear by knowing the symptoms and doing the right tests. When the question is clear, the answer is sound, and discussion of a plant preparation comes closer to what the person actually needs.

Traditional medicine uses descriptions such as “warming the kidneys” and “strengthening the spleen”. These phrases are understood within the theories in which they arose, and they differ from measuring organ function in present-day medical practice. Linking them to a specific improvement in an organ requires explanation and evidence, so that the meaning connects to a clear measure.

On blood sugar, plant research is interested in exploring compounds that may affect metabolic pathways. But the claim that a costus decoction repairs the pancreas and controls blood sugar in patients needs sufficient clinical proof. Care for people with diabetes rests on follow-up, measurement and consultation with a trusted doctor, while keeping to the prescribed treatment.

The same applies to the immune system, which is a delicate network; studying a plant’s effect on some of its markers does not mean it gives everyone a general boost. Effects of costus related to regulating some immune and inflammatory responses have been studied; these results deserve follow-up to determine their therapeutic meaning and which conditions might benefit.

An ulcer requires knowing where it is and what causes it: easing stomach pain is one thing, and proving that an ulcer has healed is another. This shows the value of careful wording: when an extract is studied in a laboratory or animal experiment, its result is reported within those limits, and judgements about treating patients rest on the appropriate studies.

The health of women and men receives particular attention in discussions of herbs, especially when having children is delayed. Infertility has many causes, and its assessment includes both partners. A plant’s possible benefit in an experiment related to the reproductive system is not enough to prove that it treats infertility, so its use should be guided after consulting a trusted doctor.

One of the most important things to understand is that costus preparations differ: the ground root, the decoction, the extract and the essential oil are not the same in composition or concentration. The name “costus oil” may be given to different products, so it is necessary to know what the product really is and the way of use intended for it, and not to assume that every oil is suitable to be taken by mouth.

The quality of a preparation begins with the correct identity of the plant, safe drying and storage, and clear information on its ingredients and source. Users have the right to know what they are taking, whether the product is a single herb or a mixture, and what it is meant for. A well-known name does not by itself reveal what a product contains; clear information is the basis of an informed choice.

The dose is not set by one rule for all people and all preparations: age, state of health, other medicines and the strength of the product all affect the decision. During pregnancy and breastfeeding, when taking medicines for a chronic illness, or when thinking of giving it to a child, consulting a trusted doctor is an essential step before use.

Practical experience has value when it is documented in a way that allows it to be understood: the diagnosis, the preparation, the dose, the duration, any other treatments, and measurements before and after use. This information helps distinguish a personal impression from a result that can be assessed, and gives researchers a clearer basis for building studies that serve patients and enrich knowledge.

The trustworthy practitioner of authentic medicine learns before he treats, trains before he prescribes preparations, and knows the limits of his specialism. Costus, like other plants, needs study that combines knowledge of the plant, the disease and the patient. In this way experience is refined, practice is disciplined, and the person’s interest comes before every other consideration.

Indian costus root is part of a plant heritage that deserves care, and the subject of research that deserves to be followed. It is truly served by verifying what is known about it, developing its study and presenting it clearly. Let the roots of knowledge be firm, the branches of research ever renewed, and their fruit the benefit of people: through knowledge words become sound, through mastery work becomes sound, and through integrity care is complete.
qust.h: Indian Costus Root: Roots in Heritage, Horizons in Research
