blocks: The thyroid gland plays a central role in regulating metabolism. Its hormones help control energy use, body temperature, and the work of the heart, intestines and nervous system, and they are also linked to reproductive health. This is why it matters to look after it with a balanced diet and suitable habits. The aim is to maintain its normal function, not to increase its activity without need.

Morning care begins with a balanced meal suited to the person’s condition and needs. It can combine a source of protein, whole grains and a portion of fruit or vegetables, with water. This habit supports overall nutrition and helps build a regular routine, without treating breakfast alone as a cure for thyroid disorders.

Dairy products such as milk, yoghurt and cheese are dietary sources of iodine, and they also provide protein and various minerals. Iodine is essential for making thyroid hormones, but the amount varies between products. Choose those that suit your needs and that you tolerate, paying attention to added sugar, fat and salt.

Eggs and fish provide useful nutrients, including iodine and selenium, in amounts that vary with the type and quantity. Egg white provides protein, and the protein in it is not a reason for the gland to weaken. Iodised salt can be used within the moderate amount recommended, without adding more salt in an attempt to stimulate the gland.

Selenium and zinc play important roles in the body’s functions and health, and both can be obtained from a varied diet that includes fish, eggs, meat, pulses and nuts. Supplements should be used only after consulting a trusted doctor to judge the need and the dose; taking more of a nutrient than you need does not mean more benefit, and it may cause harm.

Cruciferous vegetables such as cauliflower, broccoli and cabbage are part of a balanced diet. Eating them in normal food amounts does not generally call for avoiding them, especially when cooked and when iodine intake is adequate. This is different from continually eating very large amounts of them raw, especially when iodine is lacking.

The same goes for oats, unsalted nuts, and chia and flax seeds: these foods provide fibre and useful nutrients, and it is not correct to class them all as foods that suppress the thyroid when eaten in normal amounts. This also applies to berries, bananas, oranges and tomatoes. Variety and moderation are the basis of benefit, taking each person’s needs into account.

Red meat and lamb are not foods that lower thyroid activity in themselves; choosing them well depends on the amount, the fat content and the way they are prepared. With honey, chocolate and fizzy drinks, the amount of sugar and calories matters, and they should not be used as a way to regulate hormones. Nor do caffeine-free drinks weaken the gland because they lack caffeine.

Coffee and tea are not a treatment for an underactive thyroid, and caffeine can increase palpitations and nervousness in some people with an overactive thyroid. For those who take medication to replace thyroid hormone, the timing of the dose in relation to food and drink matters for its absorption, so follow the product’s instructions and the guidance of a trusted doctor.

It is essential to distinguish between an underactive and an overactive thyroid, as each has its own assessment and treatment. No single diet should be applied to everyone with a thyroid condition, and iodine supplements should not be used automatically by everyone with a thyroid disorder. Follow-up and tests determine the need, guide the decision and protect against unsuitable dietary experiments.

Care is completed by regular sleep, suitable physical activity, and keeping to the required check-ups and tests. It can help to write down your symptoms and the names of your medicines and supplements to discuss with a trusted doctor. Thyroid health benefits from a balanced plan that combines adequate nutrition, suitable treatment and regular follow-up; in this way, caring for it becomes a mindful practice that respects real needs and protects health.
thyroid.h: Thyroid Health: A Balanced Diet and Mindful Daily Habits
thyroid.by: Prepared by Dr. Yousef Ahmad Al-Maiari

blocks: Human health is a trust, and a trust is kept through knowledge and verification, and protected through awareness and good management. When recipes crowd our screens and promises of cures grow louder, a patient needs insight to guide their steps and knowledge to protect their health. A recipe’s popularity does not prove that it works, how widely it is shared does not guarantee that it is safe, and the good intentions of the person passing it on are not enough to tell who it suits and whom it may harm.

Bodies differ, their responses vary and their needs are not the same. Every person has their own state of health, age, medical history and medicines, and may have allergies or weakness in the function of certain organs. Two people may have the same pain but different causes; they may have the same named disease, yet each needs care suited to their own condition. So a herb may help one person in particular circumstances, fail to help another, and even cause harm.

Herbs contain chemical compounds, some of which have an effect on the body; that effect may be helpful or harmful, depending on the substance, its dose, how long it is used and the condition of the person taking it. The word “natural” does not mean a preparation is safe for everyone, and the presence of chemical compounds does not in itself mean it is harmful. Judgement rests on knowing the ingredients and their effects, and on weighing their benefits and risks.

Some herbs interact with medicines, making them stronger or weaker; they may affect blood pressure or blood sugar, increase the tendency to bleed, or harm the liver or kidneys. Not every herb carries all these risks, but the possibility makes a medical assessment necessary before therapeutic use, especially for pregnant and breastfeeding women, children and people with chronic illnesses.

Herbal preparations also differ in strength, purity and ingredients; they may carry the same name yet differ in their effect. Eating a plant as part of food in normal amounts is different from taking a concentrated extract of it as a treatment. And a person’s improvement after taking a herb does not by itself prove that the herb caused it, nor does it make their experience a recipe for everyone.

So before using herbs as treatment, people should consult a qualified, trusted doctor who can assess the condition and weigh the expected benefit against the possible risks. The doctor must be told about the medicines and supplements being used, and about the herbal preparation one intends to take. If it is suitable, its dose, duration and follow-up are set; if not, leaving it aside protects health. Medical supervision helps reduce risk, but it does not make every preparation guaranteed to be safe or effective.

blocks.note: No prescribed treatment should be stopped, and no necessary test delayed, in reliance on a recipe passed around. Patients deserve treatment that takes their condition into account, and decisions based on knowledge.

blocks: Whoever wishes to advise people should point them towards verification and consultation, for their words may reach someone in pain who clings to them in hope and accepts them in trust. Let words be as honest as they are influential: health is too precious to be pledged on a promise, and human life too valuable to be left to random experiment.
social.q: Herbal recipes are spreading on social media, with claims that this herb treats that disease and that one helps with this symptom. How should we deal with these recipes? Does what helps one person help another? And when can using herbs cause harm?

blocks: The humours are a concept of ancient medicine, based on the idea that health depends on the balance of four humours and disease on their imbalance: blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile. Those who held this idea gave each humour two qualities: blood was hot and moist, phlegm cold and moist, yellow bile hot and dry, and black bile cold and dry. So there are four humours, and heat, cold, moisture and dryness are qualities attributed to them in that theory, not separate humours.

These terms are understood in their historical context. Calling a person “hot” or “cold” is not a measure of their temperature, and calling them “moist” or “dry” is not a medical assessment of the fluid balance in their body. Likewise, the term “phlegm” in this theory does not necessarily match its everyday meaning today.

Take diabetes as an example. If a patient is told that sugar or sweets suit their “nature”, this should not be taken as licence to eat more of them. What matters are their blood sugar readings, the amount of carbohydrate, the medicines they use and the diet plan that suits their condition. This does not mean banning every food that contains sugar outright, but managing intake according to need and condition. A patient may need fast-acting sugar to treat a low blood sugar episode; here the need arises from a specific medical condition, not from a humoral classification.

The same is true of coffee. If it is said to suit the “temperament” of someone with high blood pressure, that phrase is not enough to decide whether it suits them. Caffeine can raise blood pressure temporarily; the response varies from person to person, and the effect may be stronger in people who do not usually drink it. So it is not right to say for certain that coffee raises everyone’s blood pressure permanently, nor that it is forbidden to everyone with high blood pressure. If it turns out that coffee raises a patient’s blood pressure or causes symptoms, its actual effect is taken into account, and a suitable amount is set, or avoiding it is decided, on the advice of their doctor.

blocks.note: When making a treatment decision, we set humoral classifications aside and look at the disease, the patient’s condition and their test results.

blocks: This principle applies in health and in illness alike: whether a food or drink is suitable is judged by reliable knowledge and its actual effect, taking each person’s individual circumstances into account. No inherited description justifies harm, and no supposed compatibility comes before the patient’s safety; what counts is what protects their health, improves their treatment and preserves their well-being.
humours.h: The humours and “body nature” versus the medical condition
humours.q: Some people say: “We treat according to the humours and the nature of the body.” What are the humours? What is meant by heat, cold, moisture and dryness? And if a food or drink is said to suit someone’s nature, but they have diabetes or high blood pressure, do we follow this classification, or do we put the needs of their medical condition first?

blocks: The salivary glands produce saliva, which keeps the mouth moist, helps with chewing, swallowing and digestion, and helps protect the teeth. The major glands lie in front of and below the ears, and under the lower jaw and tongue. Swelling of these glands is a symptom with many possible causes, not a single disease. It may come with a dry mouth, pain or difficulty opening the mouth, and the symptoms vary with the cause and how severe the condition is.

When patients notice this swelling, questions come to mind: what is causing it? How can the pain be eased? What part can herbs play? The answer begins with understanding the condition and identifying its causes. Caring for a patient combines listening well to their complaint, looking carefully at their symptoms and choosing well what suits them. So we start with the causes, then turn to ways of easing the symptoms.

Swollen salivary glands may be caused by bacterial or viral infections, blocked salivary ducts or certain immune disorders. Some herbs are used with the aim of reducing swelling and improving the flow of saliva. Herbs mentioned in this context include:

Choosing the preparation, its strength and how to use it requires a doctor’s guidance.

blocks.note: If the swelling is severe, or comes with severe pain or fever, see a trusted doctor without delay to find the exact cause and the right treatment; there may be a bacterial infection that needs medical treatment.

blocks: In an age when health trends are promoted by influencers rather than doctors, and marketing comes before accurate information, a new star has appeared: matcha, a green powder that has found its way into cafés, homes and hearts, and is sold as the elixir and the only answer for losing weight and regaining health and energy. But does matcha really do all this? Or are we facing a new wave of mass hype, driven by advertising rather than led by science?

In one consultation, a patient asked me, sincerely and with some puzzlement: “Doctor, is what they say about matcha’s role in weight loss true? Does it really deserve all this noise?” My answer was clear, based on science, not illusion; far from marketing and close to the truth. Here is the scientific account of what matcha really is, between benefit and exaggeration.

Matcha is a special kind of green tea whose leaves are finely ground; the powder is mixed directly with hot water and drunk. Matcha is believed to have originated in Japan, where it was used in meditative rituals according to the false beliefs of their practitioners. It then spread worldwide on the strength of the health properties claimed for it.

Matcha is said to contain antioxidants, vitamins and minerals that improve health and increase concentration and energy. Even so, it cannot be considered an effective treatment for weight loss, as it is promoted in some circles.

blocks.h: Matcha and weight loss: the truth behind the claims

blocks: One of the most common claims is that matcha helps weight loss by speeding up metabolism and fat burning. But how true is this? Let us look at the scientific facts:

ol: matcha contains some caffeine, which is known to increase alertness and boost fat burning temporarily. But caffeine alone does not cause large or lasting weight loss, and its effect does not compare with regular exercise or a balanced diet.

matcha contains epigallocatechin gallate (EGCG), an antioxidant believed to raise the metabolic rate. Although a few limited studies have suggested it helps fat burning, this benefit is very slight and is no quick or fundamental solution for weight loss.

preliminary studies have suggested that green tea in general may contribute to slight weight loss, but studies on matcha specifically have shown inconsistent results. Its role in reducing fat appears limited, and the available results give no conclusive evidence that it makes a noticeable difference to weight loss.

many people drink matcha with milk, sugar or artificial sweeteners. Calories can rise depending on the type and amount of these additions, which may lead to weight gain rather than loss. Anyone following a diet should therefore watch what is added to their drink.

blocks.h: Is matcha actually good for your health?

blocks: Matcha is rich in antioxidants and may help support immunity, reduce inflammation and improve mental alertness. But these benefits do not make it a substitute for a healthy lifestyle, and we should not be taken in by marketing it as a complete solution to obesity or disease.

Despite some possible health benefits, matcha is not an effective or essential means of losing weight. Marketing any product as being enough on its own to lose weight, and as a replacement for a healthy diet and exercise, is misleading marketing to beware of.
Drinking matcha in moderation can be part of a healthy lifestyle, but it is not the main way to lose weight.
matcha.h: Matcha: the new craze, between fact and misleading marketing

blocks: Among the most important and best-known possible health benefits of basil is easing swelling and inflammation: substances extracted from it have helped reduce swelling and puffiness in the body generally, and basil extract has been found to help ease the severity of joint inflammation. Its possible benefits also include an ability to fight cancer, thanks to its antioxidants and other important substances that help protect against certain types of cancer, such as lung, mouth and liver cancer.

Basil has properties that help it fight bacteria: its extracts stop bacteria from growing, so adding it to a salad is a wise way to reduce the bacteria in it. Eating basil regularly helps fight ageing and the signs of getting older and slow their pace, and it may also help fight the damage that free radicals cause in different organs of the body, such as the liver, heart and brain. This is thanks to its wealth of powerful antioxidants, which are important in fighting ageing.

Another possible benefit of basil is improving digestion, as it contains a substance that helps keep the digestive tract healthy and protect it from inflammation and other problems. It also helps maintain the acid–base balance in the body in general and the digestive tract in particular, and it is an old remedy for indigestion, bloating and fluid retention.

Basil oil and its concentrated distillate help fight depression and chronic anxiety, as they have possible effects on the body’s hormones, helping to regulate them and ensure they are produced steadily and in sufficient amounts, especially the hormones responsible for happiness. They also help reduce the production of stress and anxiety hormones.
Eating basil regularly helps slow the release of sugar into the blood, which is very important for people with diabetes, and the essential oil in its leaves helps lower triglyceride levels.

Because basil is rich in beta-carotene, its essential oil helps fight the ageing of cells that can lead to eye diseases, and its richness in vitamin A makes it especially important in fighting chronic dry eye.
Because it contains high levels of antioxidants and manganese, it helps slow the ageing of brain cells and improve brain function and cognition in general.
Basil has other benefits too, most notably strengthening the bones, easing the symptoms of premenstrual syndrome and improving metabolism, and it is also a very good source of energy.

blocks: Thalassaemia is particularly common in the Mediterranean basin, the Arab world and Asia.

There is a difference between having the disease and carrying it, depending on the deficiency or defect in the genes. A thalassaemia carrier usually has mild anaemia, and their blood cells are usually smaller than expected (microcytic anaemia), sometimes together with iron deficiency.
For those who have the disease, there are two types:

ol: usually takes the form of anaemia ranging from moderate to severe; in most cases the patient does not need blood transfusions.

known as thalassaemia major, the most serious type. It causes anaemia that begins in childhood and continues throughout the patient’s life, and it may shorten life expectancy. In this case the patient needs blood transfusions at intervals and may develop many serious complications, such as bone thinning, an enlarged spleen, malnutrition, weight loss and delayed growth. More serious still is the build-up of iron in the body caused by repeated transfusions, which is highly toxic and endangers the body and the heart. These cases can be treated with a bone marrow transplant.

blocks: In beta thalassaemia it may be important, from a nutritional point of view, to focus on how much iron enters the patient’s body through food, and to limit it as far as possible.

Bear in mind that the human body generally does not absorb large amounts of iron through the intestines, and that good-quality iron from animal sources is absorbed better than plant iron from sources such as spinach and green leafy vegetables. In addition, whenever haemoglobin levels are low, the amount of iron absorbed through the intestines rises automatically, and vice versa.

These patients should keep to the medicines that maintain the balance of the body’s iron stores and remove the excess, since iron intake should be kept below 10 milligrams a day for children under ten, and below 18 milligrams a day for those aged eleven and over.
The richest and most important sources of iron are:

ol: Liver and other organ meats, such as brain and kidneys.
Some spices, such as turmeric and cumin.

blocks: The following dietary advice and guidance may help patients with beta thalassaemia who need frequent blood transfusions:

ol: Avoid high iron levels by reducing iron intake, especially at times when haemoglobin is low.
Eat white meat instead of red meat, which is rich in iron; white meat contains less of it.
Drink tea with meals, as tea contains substances that bind to iron and prevent the body from absorbing it.

Drink milk, or cook with milk and dairy products, alongside iron sources, as they prevent iron from being absorbed. But calcium intake should be kept up and attention paid to its sources, to reduce the risk of bone thinning and its problems.
Do not eat foods rich in vitamin C, such as citrus fruit, with iron-containing foods, as vitamin C encourages and increases iron absorption.
Some whole grains, such as wheat, oats and soya, prevent iron from being absorbed in the intestines and limit the role of vitamin C in increasing and encouraging iron absorption.
Drinking coffee may help reduce iron absorption.
Read the nutrition labels on all foods and check their iron content.

blocks: It is inflammation of the liver caused by infection with one of the five hepatitis viruses. In most people it starts suddenly and lasts only a few weeks.
Cases range from no symptoms at all to very severe symptoms. Infected people may have a poor appetite, nausea, vomiting, fever, pain in the upper right part of the abdomen, and jaundice.
Acute viral hepatitis is common all over the world. Most cases clear up on their own, but some persist and worsen until they become chronic hepatitis.
Acute viral hepatitis can be caused by five main hepatitis viruses:

Hepatitis A is the most common cause of acute hepatitis, followed by hepatitis B. Other viruses can also cause acute viral hepatitis, including the Epstein–Barr virus (EBV), which causes infectious mononucleosis.
Certain activities, such as getting a tattoo or body piercing, sharing needles to inject drugs, using cannabis, or having several sexual partners, increase the risk of hepatitis.

Acute viral hepatitis can cause anything from a mild, flu-like illness to fatal liver failure, and sometimes there are no symptoms at all. The severity of symptoms and the speed of recovery vary greatly with the virus causing the infection and the person’s reaction to it.

Hepatitis A and C cause very mild symptoms or none at all, and symptoms may come and go unnoticed. Hepatitis B and E are more likely to cause severe symptoms. Infection with hepatitis B and D at the same time, known as co-infection, can make the symptoms of hepatitis B more severe.
Symptoms of acute viral hepatitis usually begin suddenly and include:

ol: A general feeling of being unwell (malaise).
Pain in the upper right part of the abdomen, where the liver lies.

blocks: A distaste for cigarettes is a typical symptom in smokers. Infected people, especially those with hepatitis B, may have joint pain and, from time to time, red itchy hives.

The urine sometimes becomes dark and the stools pale after three to ten days. Jaundice may develop, meaning the skin and the whites of the eyes turn yellow, sometimes together with itching. These symptoms happen because the damaged liver cannot clear bilirubin from the blood as it normally does.

Bilirubin is a yellow pigment produced when haemoglobin, the part of red blood cells that carries oxygen, breaks down as part of the normal recycling of old or damaged red blood cells. Bilirubin then builds up in the blood and is deposited in the skin, making it look yellow and causing itching, and in the whites of the eyes, making them look yellow.

Bilirubin is normally released into the intestine as part of bile, the yellow-green digestive fluid made by the liver, and passed out in the stools, which gives them their typical brown colour. In people with hepatitis the stools are pale because bilirubin does not reach the intestine to be passed out. Instead it is passed in the urine, making it dark. The liver may be enlarged and tender to the touch.

Most of the early symptoms, such as loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting and fever, usually clear within a week, and people feel better even though the jaundice may get worse. Jaundice usually peaks within one to two weeks and then fades over two to four weeks or more. But full recovery can sometimes take much longer.

Fulminant hepatitis occurs in rare cases. It is severe hepatitis with signs of liver failure. It can occur in people with hepatitis A, but it is more likely in people with hepatitis B, especially if they also have hepatitis D.

Fulminant hepatitis can progress very quickly, and the liver becomes unable to make enough of the proteins that help the blood clot. However, even though the blood cannot clot normally, people do not bruise or bleed more easily or without cause.

The liver cannot remove toxic substances as it usually does, so these build up in the blood and reach the brain, causing hepatic encephalopathy. People may deteriorate and fall into a coma within days to weeks. Fulminant hepatitis can be fatal, especially in adults.

People with acute viral hepatitis usually recover within four to eight weeks, even without treatment. But people infected with hepatitis C may become carriers of the virus. Adults infected with hepatitis B are less likely to become carriers.

Carriers have no symptoms, even though they remain infected and can pass the virus on to others. Carriers may develop chronic hepatitis even though they show no signs of illness, and eventually they may develop cirrhosis (severe scarring of the liver) or liver cancer.

Doctors suspect acute viral hepatitis from the symptoms. During the examination the doctor presses on the abdomen over the liver, which is tender and somewhat enlarged in about 50% of people with acute viral hepatitis.
Doctors suspect fulminant hepatitis when:

ol: A person is seriously ill and develops jaundice very quickly.
Results of blood-clotting tests, such as the prothrombin time or the international normalised ratio (INR), are abnormal.
The condition of a person with liver disease begins to worsen quickly.

blocks: Investigation for acute viral hepatitis usually begins with blood tests to see how well the liver is working and whether it is damaged.

Liver function tests measure the levels of liver enzymes and other substances the liver produces. These tests can show inflammation of the liver and often help doctors tell hepatitis caused by alcohol or drug misuse from hepatitis caused by a viral infection.

Diagnosing fulminant hepatitis requires liver tests to see how quickly the blood clots, because fulminant hepatitis stops the blood from clotting normally. If acute viral hepatitis seems likely, it may then be possible to find its cause.

To find out whether the condition has a cause other than a virus, the doctor may ask about any medicines the person uses that can cause hepatitis, such as isoniazid, used to treat tuberculosis, and about how much alcohol they drink.
Because treatments for viral hepatitis are only partly effective, preventing it is extremely important.
Preventive measures against infection with hepatitis viruses include:

ol: Washing hands well before handling food.
Not sharing needles to inject drugs.
Not sharing toothbrushes, razors or other items that can carry blood.

blocks: Most people with acute viral hepatitis need no special treatment. However, people with severe acute hepatitis may need their mental state to be monitored. People with hepatitis are asked not to drink alcohol.
An infected liver may not process medicines normally. The doctor may need to stop a medicine that could build up to harmful levels in the body, or reduce its dose, such as warfarin or theophylline.

blocks.note: For this reason, people with hepatitis are asked to tell their doctor about all the medicines they use, whether prescription or over-the-counter, including medicinal herbs, so that doses can be adjusted when necessary.

blocks: The albumin (ALB) blood test is an important test used to measure the amount of albumin in your blood. Albumin is a protein made by the liver; it helps keep fluid in the bloodstream so that it does not leak into other tissues. It also carries various substances around the body, including hormones, vitamins and enzymes.
Low levels of albumin in the blood can point to a problem with the liver or kidneys.

blocks.h: What the albumin test is used for

blocks: The blood albumin test is a type of liver function test: blood tests that measure various enzymes and proteins in the liver, including albumin. The albumin test may also be part of a comprehensive metabolic panel, a group of tests that measure many substances in your blood, including electrolytes, glucose and proteins such as albumin.

blocks.h: Why do I need an albumin test?

blocks: Your doctor may have ordered liver function tests, which include albumin, as part of a routine check-up. You may also need this test if you have symptoms of liver or kidney disease.

ol: Jaundice, a condition in which your skin and eyes turn yellow.
Swelling around the abdomen and thighs, or in the face.
Passing urine often, especially at night.
Foamy or bloody urine, or urine the colour of coffee.

Levels higher than normal may point to dehydration or severe diarrhoea.

blocks.note: If your albumin levels are not within the normal range, this does not necessarily mean you have a condition that needs treatment. Some medicines, including steroids, insulin and hormones, can raise albumin levels, while others, including birth control pills, can lower them.

blocks: Lupus is an autoimmune disease that causes many effects in different parts of the body. Below are the key facts about lupus erythematosus, commonly known simply as lupus.

Lupus is a chronic autoimmune disease, which means the immune system attacks healthy tissue; this can cause inflammation and pain in any part of the body. Lupus most commonly affects the following parts of the body:

Because lupus affects many parts of the body, it can cause many different symptoms. There is no single known cause of the autoimmune process behind lupus; it is not caused by infectious bacteria, and it does not pass from one person to another.
There are several types of lupus, including:

ol: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), one of the most common types.
Cutaneous lupus, which affects only the skin.
Drug-induced lupus, a lupus-like illness caused by certain prescribed medicines.
Neonatal lupus, a rare condition affecting the babies of women with lupus.

blocks: The general symptoms associated with lupus include:

ol: A facial rash known as the butterfly rash.
Poor circulation in the fingers and toes on exposure to cold, known as Raynaud’s phenomenon.

blocks: Factors that make lupus more likely include:

ol: Hormonal changes, such as those that happen at puberty.

blocks: To be diagnosed with lupus, a patient must have four of eleven common signs of the disease. Tests used to diagnose lupus may include:

ol: Imaging of the heart, brain, lungs, joints, muscles or intestines.

blocks: The aim of treatment is to control the symptoms, and a patient with lupus needs ongoing assessment and follow-up by specialists.
Possible complications of lupus include:

ol: Blood clots and inflammation of the blood vessels.

It has a distinctive appearance that resembles a lion’s mane or feathers, and it is regarded as a mushroom with many health benefits. Some of these benefits are:

it contains compounds that can stimulate the growth and renewal of nerve cells, helping to improve memory and concentration.
it has anti-inflammatory and antibacterial properties that may help treat digestive problems such as ulcers and intestinal inflammation.
lion’s mane boosts immunity by stimulating the activity of the white blood cells that fight infection.
some studies have shown that certain compounds in lion’s mane can inhibit the growth of cancer cells.
it may help ease symptoms of anxiety and depression through its effect on nerve-cell growth and nervous balance.
it has antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties that may help lower harmful cholesterol and improve the health of the heart and blood vessels.

blocks: The kidneys are essential organs that keep the body in balance and its internal environment stable. They work constantly, and their functions go beyond making urine to regulating fluids, minerals and blood pressure. Supporting their work means keeping them working efficiently and protecting them from damage. Caring for them rests on balanced nutrition, healthy habits and follow-up suited to each person’s condition and needs.

blocks.h: 1. Filtering the blood and removing waste

blocks: The kidneys filter the blood through tiny units called nephrons. In this process they separate out waste and excess water and return to the blood most of the water and the substances the body needs. The remaining waste and fluid collect to form urine, which passes through the ureters to the bladder.

The kidneys help regulate the amount of water in the body and control the levels of sodium, potassium, calcium and phosphorus. This balance is essential for the heart, muscles and nerves to work. The kidneys also remove excess acid and help maintain the balance between acidity and alkalinity in the blood.

blocks.h: 3. Helping regulate blood pressure and support blood and bone health

blocks: The kidneys have an important hormonal role: they help regulate blood pressure, stimulate the production of red blood cells and help keep the bones strong. So when kidney function declines, problems in these areas may appear, along with a build-up of waste and fluid.

The kidneys benefit from a balanced diet that helps control blood pressure, blood sugar and weight. For a person with healthy kidneys this includes a variety of vegetables and fruit, whole grains and suitable sources of protein, with less salt, added sugar and saturated fat. The benefit comes from combining these choices and keeping to them.

Reading nutrition labels helps you know how much salt, sugar and fat foods contain, and cooking at home helps you control ingredients and amounts. You can grill or bake instead of deep-frying, choose foods low in added sugar, and eat whole fruit instead of juice. These habits support overall health and help control the factors that can harm the kidneys.

Useful examples include apples, berries and strawberries, which provide fibre, vitamins and antioxidants. They can be included in meals in suitable amounts, without adding a lot of sugar. A variety of vegetables provides fibre, minerals and vitamins and helps build a balanced meal that meets the body’s needs.

No single food treats all kidney diseases, and a food being rich in antioxidants does not mean it restores damaged kidney function. The foundation is a varied diet suited to the person’s condition, respecting any dietary limits set by the disease or indicated by test results.

Whole grains such as oats and brown rice are sources of fibre and minerals. Fish, eggs and pulses can be suitable sources of protein within a balanced plan. Unsaturated fats such as olive oil help support the health of the heart and blood vessels. Amounts are set according to nutritional needs and state of health.

Drinking a suitable amount of water helps avoid dehydration and is one of the most important ways of preventing kidney stones. How much fluid a person needs depends on their condition, activity and the weather. People with kidney failure or fluid build-up, however, may need to limit how much they drink according to their medical assessment; drinking a lot of water is not right for everyone.

For those who have had stones before, the diet is based on the type of stone. Some patients may need to reduce sodium, animal protein or foods rich in oxalates. With some types of stone, getting enough calcium from food is part of prevention, so it should not automatically be restricted for all patients.

blocks.h: 8. Tailoring the diet for kidney patients

blocks: A kidney patient may need to control potassium, phosphorus, protein and fluids according to their test results. High potassium can affect the heart and muscles, and a build-up of phosphorus can harm the bones and blood vessels. Blanket food bans are not imposed on all patients; restrictions are set according to actual need, taking care to avoid malnutrition.

Protein needs differ before and after starting dialysis: some patients may need moderate amounts, while those on dialysis need more. Salt substitutes may contain potassium, so they should not be used automatically. Reading the ingredients of processed foods helps identify added phosphates and sodium and choose what fits the diet plan.

blocks.h: 9. Habits that keep the kidneys working well

blocks: Kidney care is completed by controlling blood sugar and blood pressure, keeping a healthy weight, staying physically active, stopping smoking and avoiding frequent use of certain painkillers without supervision. Early kidney disease may cause no clear symptoms, so suitable tests, especially for people with diabetes or high blood pressure, help detect damage and start care early.

blocks.note: Note: bodies differ in their nature, needs and state of health, so every patient has a treatment and diet plan suited to them, set according to their diagnosis, test results and response to treatment.

Cupping stimulates the memory, increases concentration and energy, relieves mental and nervous illnesses, and brings calm and rest to the nerves. It also treats dental problems, relieves nerve inflammation, protects against high blood pressure, hemiplegia and vaginal bleeding, and relieves psychological stress, fatigue, insomnia and exhaustion. It improves blood flow to the brain, thereby increasing concentration and energy, protects against cancer, and guards against rheumatism, joint disease and paralysis.

Cupping stimulates the lymphatic and blood circulation, relieves pressure on the nerves and provokes reactions in the body, which helps the brain pay more attention to the organs so that it sends the necessary instructions to the body’s systems to take suitable action. It clears the effects of toxins and harmful medicines from the body, strengthens immunity and protects against serious diseases.

Cupping helps the body get rid of corrupt blood containing microbes and germs, helps activate the body’s organs and functions, and increases the delivery of oxygen to the organs concerned. blocks: Manuka has many benefits, ranging from cosmetic and therapeutic benefits to benefits for hormonal balance and for pregnant women, as well as many others.

Many people prefer natural products to manufactured ones, especially when it comes to the skin and skin care. Natural products such as honey are therefore widely used as an alternative to ointments and therapeutic formulations, or even to cosmetics, because of the negative side effects the chemicals in those products may have.

Manuka honey is the most beneficial kind of honey in particular, and of natural products in general, in this respect. Its benefit far exceeds that of any other kind of honey, thanks to the antioxidant, antibacterial and anti-inflammatory substances it contains, such as hydrogen peroxide and methylglyoxal. Manuka honey can be used on the skin for therapeutic or preventive purposes, or for regular skin care.
Manuka distillate is very effective at preserving the hair and protecting it from hair loss and dryness. Its benefits include:

ol: Restoring the hair’s natural rate of growth.
Giving every hair a touch of shine and fullness.

blocks: Using manuka honey on your hair is very easy; you can:

ol: Mix a little of it with the shampoo you normally use.
Mix manuka honey with manuka distillate and olive oil, and apply the mixture to dried hair for thirty minutes.
Then wash your hair with ordinary shampoo, or shampoo mixed with manuka distillate, and enjoy hair as soft as silk.

blocks: Manuka has a clear effect on the activity of the hormone oestrogen, which points to remarkable and direct benefits of manuka products for hormonal balance in the body.
But how do we use manuka for this? We will soon publish many manuka recipes, but it is enough to add it to your breakfast.

Another benefit of manuka, as mentioned above, is that it fights bacteria. Its benefits do not stop there: it is also excellent for maintaining the body’s immune system, and a strong immune system is the key to hormonal balance.

The definite answer is yes. It is not only suitable but extremely important, and manuka is completely safe for pregnant mothers. Manuka honey and its distillate are an excellent alternative to all other forms of medicine used during pregnancy; because they are entirely natural, they have no negative side effects, and so they are of great benefit to pregnant women.

blocks: Scientific and practical trials have shown that taking olive leaves may help prevent or delay the onset of diabetes and lower blood sugar, by bringing blood glucose back to normal levels and limiting the damage caused by the blood sugar spikes that people with diabetes experience. Reduced sensitivity to insulin and a reduced response from the pancreas are important factors in the development of type 2 diabetes.

This is what blood sugar tests have shown: a marked fall in blood sugar after taking olive leaves or an olive-leaf decoction, at a rate comparable to, and sometimes greater than, the fall produced by insulin injections. This is attributed to several mechanisms: olive leaves slow the conversion of starches into simple sugars, slow the absorption of sugars in the intestine and increase the uptake of glucose from the blood by the tissues. They also raise the levels of natural antioxidants and protect the tissues from oxidative damage, including the damage that occurs when glucose binds to them.

Continued use of olive leaf and its decoction may therefore be an alternative, natural treatment for people with diabetes, together with regular blood sugar tests three to four hours after drinking olive-leaf tea, and a diet based on giving up simple sugars and refined sugar, such as table sugar, altogether, and eating limited amounts of starches instead.

blocks.note: However, people with diabetes must consult a specialist doctor before using olive leaf as a treatment, and they are also asked not to take olive leaves at the same time as insulin injections or diabetes medicines, to avoid a severe drop in blood sugar and serious complications.
